asDecan.p: Your Sun sits in the last ten degrees of Pisces, from twenty to twenty-nine, at the tail end of the zodiac, and the Golden Dawn gives that slice to Mars. Pisces is mutable water, ruled by Jupiter in the old scheme and Neptune in the modern one, and it soaks up everyone's feelings along with its own. Mars has no dignity there, good or bad. It's a guest in Jupiter's house, neither helped nor held back, and it picks up the manners of the place, so its push comes out generous and mostly gets spent on other people. The first decan is Saturn's, with the Eight of Cups, someone walking away from what isn't enough. The middle one is Jupiter's, with the Nine, sitting back pleased with what's been gathered. Yours is the only one of the three with much fight in it, and it's already leaning toward Aries, the sign Mars rules. The Moon is still your Sun card. The Ten is the closer look at your ten degrees.

A friend mentions over dinner that her rent's gone up, and by the weekend you've sent her three listings and offered to drive her to the inspections. Most people would have said how awful and changed the subject. At a family Christmas where two of your siblings aren't speaking, you seat them side by side and carry the conversation for two hours so the lunch works. Someone at work gets left off the Friday drinks invite, you notice, and next week they're on it without anyone knowing who sorted it. I see this a lot with late Pisces Suns. You cry at adverts and at other people's weddings, and you're soft in all the ways people expect from the sign. What they don't expect is how fast you move once a feeling has told you something needs doing, and on a Sunday with nothing planned you're usually restless by eleven.

You're good at the hard end of things, the part of a crisis most people hope someone else will handle. When a mate's dad is in hospital for a month, you set up the roster of who's bringing meals and run it in the group chat with enough jokes that nobody feels organised. A family has to clear out a parent's house, and you're there on the Saturday with boxes and a rough plan, and you still let everyone stop and cry over the photo albums. Pisces is the last sign, and Mars in its last ten degrees has the energy to do the work of an ending while the Pisces in you feels all of it. Retirement lunches, the last night before a friend moves to London, you make those go well, down to who sits next to whom.

Look at the card, the couple with their arms up under a rainbow of cups and the two kids dancing beside them. You carry a version of that picture around and work hard to make real life match it. You book the family holiday, the cabin, the long lunch, and you're hurt when your teenager stays in the room on their phone, because the picture never had room for anyone's actual mood. The other version is harder to spot. Mars likes a cause, and Pisces feels for whoever's losing, so you can keep backing someone long after they've stopped trying. The cousin you've lent money to four times. The friend who's been about to leave the same bad relationship for three years, whose call you still take every Sunday. Some of that is loyalty. Some of it is that saying no to someone who's struggling feels like being cruel.

When something breaks, a relationship ending, a parent getting sick, missing out on a role you'd earned, you look after everyone else first. You're on the phone to your brother checking he's all right before you've taken it in yourself. A week later the energy that was going outward has nowhere to go, and it turns into a lot of sleep or a sudden burst of doing. You repaint the hallway, sign up for a course, pick a fight about the dishwasher that has nothing to do with the dishwasher. People close to you find it confusing, because you seemed fine and then you weren't, and they tend to get the anger without hearing what it's about. What helps is getting the Mars side into your body. A hard swim, a long walk up a steep hill, then saying out loud to one person what you're actually angry about.

A lot of Pisces wait to be asked. You usually don't. You'll send the first message, suggest the second date, and say how you feel a few weeks before it's sensible, and that's the Mars in this decan. Within a few months you've started building a life around the two of you, the friends they should meet, a Sunday routine, the idea of a dog. You also tend to fall for the family that comes with a person. You want the long lunches at their parents' place, and you remember their nan's birthday without being told. That's lovely if they're close to their people. If they aren't, or they've spent years getting some distance, your keenness can feel like pressure, and they may not be able to explain why. Ask early how they feel about their family, and follow their lead on how much of it you see.

You work best where there's a group of people to look after and a real aim to push toward. Nursing, teaching, running a café, social work, a small team that's had a bad run and needs someone to steady it, events, anything where the mood of the place matters and somebody has to hold it. You're good in a crisis because you stay kind while things are moving fast, and people notice that on the worst days. It goes wrong when the team's feelings become your job. You stay late smoothing over a row between two colleagues that the manager should have handled, and you do it for years without asking for the title or the money that ought to come with it. You'll fight hard for a client, or for a junior who's being underpaid. Asking for your own rise is the Mars move you tend to skip.

At twenty this decan looks like a lot of feeling with the drive pointed at other people's lives. You're the friend who helps everyone move house and still hasn't worked out what you want to study. The Mars side comes in bursts, months of effort on a relationship or a cause, then a crash. By the mid-thirties most people with it have found something of their own to build, a family, a home, a group of friends that's lasted, and the push steadies because it has somewhere to go. That's often when the Ten of Cups starts to look like your actual life. The fifties tend to bring a loosening. The kids leave or the work settles, and I've seen plenty of late Pisces people turn that energy on themselves for the first time and be surprised by what they want. Often it has some Aries in it, a trek, a business, a boat.

When someone you love is having a rough time, ask them one question before you do anything: do you want help, or do you want company? Then do what they say. If it's company, sit with them and don't fix anything, even when you can see exactly what needs doing. Try it for a month with everyone, your partner, the kids, the friend who rings on Sundays. Keep a rough count. Company usually wins, and the people you love tend to be steadier than you'd given them credit for.
